query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin aluminide coating (via pack cementation) to cast HfNbTaTiZr will enable the formation of a protective, adherent Al2O3 scale during high‐temperature exposure that suppresses internal oxidation without altering the bulk’s favorable mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin aluminide coating on the alloy surface by pack cementation.
generation.conditions: Test the coated alloy at 1000 °C in air for extended durations (e.g., 100 hours) under strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1 for high-temperature strength and in room-temperature tensile tests to assess ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: The aluminide coating oxidizes to form a continuous, adherent Al2O3 layer that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Upon exposure to high-temperature oxidizing conditions, the pre-applied aluminide coating rapidly converts to a stable Al2O3 scale that minimizes further oxygen ingress. This barrier prevents deleterious oxidation of the bulk alloy while the underlying microstructure remains unchanged, preserving ductility and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit markedly improved oxygen resistance (e.g., thinner oxide layers and reduced internal oxidation) at 1000 °C compared to untreated samples, while retaining the baseline mechanical performance in tensile tests at room temperature and high temperature.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy shows poor oxygen resistance with significant oxidation under high-temperature exposure despite having acceptable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for the material’s performance at 1000 °C in air (within strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1 for strength measurements) and for room-temperature ductility benchmarks of 8–16%. It does not address potential long-term diffusion alterations beyond the experimental time frame.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the long-term adhesion of the alumina scale at prolonged high-temperature exposures and whether any interdiffusion at the coating–substrate interface might eventually alter mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample groups of cast HfNbTaTiZr alloys: one group receives the thin aluminide coating via pack cementation and the other remains untreated. Expose both groups to 1000 °C in an oxidizing (air) atmosphere for 100 hours. After exposure, conduct tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C, and perform microstructural analyses (using SEM/EDS) to measure oxide layer thickness and investigate coating integrity.
measurements: Tensile ductility and yield strength at room temperature
Microstructural phase analysis of the coating/substrate interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminide-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide formation compared to untreated samples, or if the mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) of the coated samples deteriorate relative to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 (equiatomic atomic percentages). Processing: Vacuum arc melting (4 re-melts), casting into bars (gravity or suction-assisted), followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests at room temperature, and creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa loads.
